vignette:
Amit was 35 when he first came for help, a married South Asian tax consultant who had spent several months, early in his career, doing relief work in a war zone. He had gone there believing he would be useful in a place where everything had been broken apart. What he brought back instead was a set of memories that arrived out of order and without warning, along with a conviction that he had failed in the one role that mattered most. When he spoke about that period, he did not tell the story smoothly. He would stop, restart, and then describe fragments: the sharp smell of smoke hanging over damaged buildings, people crying at funerals, the sight of graves and new earth, and the faces of people who had been angry in the middle of chaos. He said the memories never seemed to line up properly in his mind. He could not place events in the right sequence, and that confusion made the whole period feel unreal and unfinished, as if it were still happening somewhere just beyond reach.

During the relief work, Amit had moved through sites where smoke and fire were common enough that the smell became tied to fear in his body. Even years later, a whiff of smoke from a kitchen mishap, a bonfire, or a passing car could bring him back so abruptly that he felt exposed and unsteady. He also found funerals and cemeteries deeply difficult. He described arriving at grief-related events and immediately wanting to leave, because the sight of mourning faces and graves made the past crowd in around him. At such moments, he felt pulled back into the role he had occupied then, standing in places where life had already been lost and where he believed he should have done more. He had come to believe that the world no longer worked by any rules he could trust. What had once seemed orderly, predictable, and understandable now felt completely broken in his mind. He said that after that experience he no longer felt simply changed; he felt set apart, as if other people were living inside a world that still made sense while he remained outside it.

There were also moments when other people’s anger, even when voiced calmly, brought on a wave of tension and alarm. In his present work as a tax consultant, this showed up in ordinary office interactions: a client speaking sharply about a return, a colleague sounding irritated over email, a manager questioning a deadline. Amit would notice his body tightening before he had even understood what was being said. He often covered his face with his hands in those moments, a small reflex he said made him feel briefly less visible. At work, this could leave him staring down at papers while his mind emptied out, making it hard to concentrate on numbers, forms, or instructions. He was embarrassed by that difficulty because his job depended on sustained attention, and he worried that others would assume he was careless or inattentive. He did not say this happened every day, but he described it as enough of a problem that he had begun double-checking the same documents repeatedly, losing time and confidence.

At home, Amit’s sense of safety was not the same at night as it was during the day. He found himself listening more intently after dark, startled by ordinary sounds that would not bother most people: a door closing in the hallway, a pot dropped in the kitchen, a phone vibrating on a table. He jumped before he could stop himself, then felt foolish for reacting so strongly. Nighttime had become the period when his mind seemed to wander most easily toward the war zone and the people he believed he had not protected. He avoided anything that might make him feel happy or hopeful, saying that positive moments felt fragile and almost dangerous, as if expecting something good was another way to invite its loss. Even with his wife, who had tried to be patient, he found himself pulling back from plans or celebrations. He would decline outings, cut conversations short, or quietly step away when the mood became festive. The result was a life that had grown narrower and more solitary, and he was aware of that distance. He said he felt isolated and set apart from other people, including those who cared about him, because they could not fully understand what he carried.

The most painful part, he said, was what happened when the memories returned uninvited. He felt intense shame when he remembered the events, not only sadness or fear. At times, the memory came with such bodily force that he felt as if his body were back in the same position it had been in during the frightening event, frozen in place by what he had seen and what he had not been able to do. He understood this as his own failure. He was certain that he should have protected others and that he had not. That belief sat heavily on him through the years, surfacing especially around smoke, funerals, anger, and the quiet of night. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing sense that he could not keep moving through work and marriage while carrying all of this alone. He wanted the memories to become less overwhelming and less shame-filled, and he was most afraid that, if nothing changed, he would remain trapped outside his own life, unable to feel safe, useful, or connected again.
